corpus_definition: Always behaving or happening in the same way.

forms.definition: the quality of always doing something in the same good way
forms.example: The coach praised the consistency of her training.
forms.note: Consistency also means how thick or smooth a liquid is: 'soup with a creamy consistency'.

syn.note: Close: you can trust someone to do well every time.
Related: something happens at the same times or in the same way.
Related: not changing suddenly; used more for prices, health or countries.

ant.note: Changing from good to bad, so people cannot depend on you.

forms.definition: to be made of certain parts or things
forms.example: The test consists of three parts: reading, writing and speaking.
forms.note: Belongs to the old meaning of the family (be made of, usually 'consist of'), not to 'always the same'. There is no verb meaning 'make consistent'.

forms.definition: always behaving or happening in the same way
forms.example: She is a consistent worker who meets all deadlines.

syn.note: Close: you can trust the person or thing to do well every time.
Easy word: not changing much, going on in the same way.
Related: happening at the same times again and again.
Related: happening all the time or not changing at all.
Very close to reliable; used about people and machines.

ant.note: Sometimes good and sometimes bad, so you cannot depend on it.
You cannot trust it to work or to do well.

forms.definition: in the same way every time, again and again
forms.example: Aziz has consistently got top marks in maths this year.

syn.note: Easy word; consistently suggests a steady pattern over time.
Related: often and at the same times.
In a way that people can trust every time.

ant.note: Sometimes one way and sometimes another.

context.text: Dilnoza is a consistent student. She has consistently done her homework every evening, and her teacher says this consistency is why her English is so good.

reviewer_note: consist is shown as other_meaning (be made of); consistency also has a 'thickness' sense, mentioned in a note.

corpus_definition: The body of a person who has passed away.

forms.definition: the body of a dead person
forms.example: The police found a corpse near the river.

syn.note: Same meaning and easier; used in everyday speech.
Common in news: 'a body was found'. Can also mean a living body.
Formal: what is left of a dead person, often after a long time.
The dead body of an animal, not usually a person.

forms.note: There is no verb made from corpse.
There is no common adjective made from corpse. Use dead.
There is no adverb made from corpse.

context.text: In the detective story, a corpse is found in an old house in Bukhara. Nobody knows who the dead man is.

reviewer_note: Single-form word. corps (a group of soldiers) looks similar but is a different word; left out.

corpus_definition: To break into very small pieces.

forms.definition: a very small piece of bread, cake or biscuit
forms.example: There were crumbs all over the table after breakfast.
forms.note: The b is silent: /krʌm/. crumble is made from this word.

syn.note: Easy, general word for a small piece of anything.
A part of something; it can be big or small.
A very small spot or piece, like dust.

forms.definition: a sweet dish of baked fruit covered with a dry mix of flour, butter and sugar
forms.example: My British friend made an apple crumble for dessert.
forms.note: Belongs to crumble = a dessert (mainly British English), not the act of breaking into pieces.

forms.definition: to break, or make something break, into very small pieces
forms.example: The dry cake began to crumble away.
forms.note: Also used for buildings or systems that slowly fall apart: 'The old wall is crumbling.'

syn.note: Easy phrasal verb: to break into many pieces.
Easy: to break into pieces, often because something is old.
Formal: to break into many small parts and stop existing.
Related: to fall down suddenly, like a building.
To press something hard so it breaks; you crush it, it crumbles.

forms.definition: breaking easily into very small pieces
forms.example: This cheese is soft and crumbly.

syn.note: Easy word: food that is dry often breaks into pieces.
Hard but breaking easily, like thin glass or old bones.

ant.note: Hard and firm, not breaking easily.

forms.definition: slowly breaking into pieces, often because it is very old
forms.example: We walked past the crumbling walls of the old fortress.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from crumble.

context.text: Grandma's cake was so crumbly that it crumbled in my hand. Soon there were crumbs all over the carpet.

reviewer_note: crumb is the base word (crumble is made from it); crumble as a dessert noun is other_meaning. No affix claimed: crumbl-y does not split cleanly.

corpus_definition: The young offspring of certain wild animals.

forms.definition: a baby bear, lion, tiger, fox or wolf
forms.example: The bear cub played near its mother.

syn.note: Easy phrase; cub is used only for some wild animals.
Formal noun for the babies of any animal: 'a lion and her young'.
A baby dog, seal or wolf.
A baby cat, not a wild animal.

forms.note: Cub as a verb (to give birth to cubs) is very rare and not in learner dictionaries.
There is no adjective made from cub.
There is no adverb made from cub.

context.text: At the Tashkent Zoo, the lioness has two new cubs. Children love to watch the little cub play with its mother's tail.

reviewer_note: Single-form word. cub reporter and Cub Scout are compounds and left out.

corpus_definition: To prepare land and grow crops on it.

forms.definition: the work of preparing land and growing crops on it
forms.example: Cotton cultivation is important in many parts of Uzbekistan.

syn.note: Easy, everyday word for growing crops and keeping animals.
The whole activity or science of farming in a country.
Easy: 'the growing of rice'.

forms.definition: to prepare land and grow crops on it
forms.example: The farmers cultivate corn on their large land.
forms.note: It also means to try to develop a skill or a friendship: 'cultivate good relations'.

syn.note: Easy word: you grow a plant; you cultivate land or a crop.
Easy word: to use land for crops or animals.
To put seeds or young plants in the ground; only the first step.
Old-fashioned: to prepare land for crops by digging.

ant.note: To not look after something, so land becomes wild.

forms.definition: used for growing crops, not wild
forms.example: Most of the cultivated land in the valley grows cotton and wheat.
forms.note: Cultivated can also describe a person who is well educated and has good manners.

syn.note: Easy: used for farming.
With plants or seeds put in it.

ant.note: Growing naturally, without help from people.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from cultivate.

people.definition: a machine or tool that breaks up soil before planting
people.example: The farmer used a cultivator to prepare the field.
people.note: It can also mean a person who grows crops, but this is rare.

context.text: In spring, farmers in the Fergana Valley cultivate cotton and vegetables. Careful cultivation makes the land rich, and the cultivated fields look green all summer.

reviewer_note: Map keeps the farming sense; the 'develop a skill/friendship' sense is only in a note. culture shares an old root but is not made from cultivate, so it is left out.

corpus_definition: Increasing by adding more parts together over time.

forms.note: There is no common noun made from cumulative. Accumulation (from accumulate) has a similar meaning but is a different word.
There is no verb made from cumulative. Accumulate has a similar meaning and an old shared root, but cumulative is not made from it.

forms.definition: growing bigger as more parts are added over time
forms.example: The cumulative effect of pollution is damaging the environment.

syn.note: Easy word: getting bigger; it does not say how.
Getting bigger or more over time.
Close: collected or built up over a long time.
The whole amount when everything is added; it does not show growth.

forms.definition: when all the parts are added together over time
forms.example: Small savings, cumulatively, can pay for a new car.

syn.note: Easy word: when things are added or taken as one.
When everything is counted.

context.text: One cigarette may not seem dangerous, but the cumulative damage over many years is serious. Cumulatively, small habits change our health.

reviewer_note: accumulate/accumulation kept out as not_family (same Latin root, not made from cumulative); listed accumulated only as a synonym.

corpus_definition: Clever at getting what you want, often by tricking others.

forms.definition: the skill of getting what you want by tricking people
forms.example: The thief used all his cunning to escape from the police.

syn.note: Using tricks to get what you want.
Being clever, in a good or bad way.
Very close: being clever in a secret, dishonest way.

ant.note: Telling the truth and not tricking people.

forms.note: There is no verb made from cunning.

forms.definition: clever at getting what you want, often by tricking others
forms.example: The cunning fox escaped the trap easily.

syn.note: Very close: clever and secret, often in a dishonest way.
Very close: good at tricking people.
Doing things secretly to trick people.
Easy word: good at thinking; clever is usually positive, cunning is often negative.
Easy word: quick at thinking; usually positive.

ant.note: Telling the truth and not tricking others.
Too ready to believe people, easy to trick.

forms.definition: in a clever way that tricks or surprises people
forms.example: The door was cunningly hidden behind a bookcase.

syn.note: Easy and more positive.
In a secret, tricky way.

ant.note: In a true and open way, without tricks.

context.text: In Uzbek folk tales, the fox is always cunning. It cunningly tricks the other animals, but in the end its cunning does not help it.

reviewer_note: Noun cunning is a zero-change conversion; no -ing affix claimed (cunning is not 'cun' + -ing).

corpus_definition: The virtual place where computer users communicate and share information.

forms.definition: the online world where computer users meet and share information
forms.example: Much of our life is now spent in cyberspace.

syn.note: Everyday word; cyberspace sounds more like an imagined place.
Informal, common word for the internet and its websites.
Easy phrase with almost the same meaning.
A world made by computers, often in a game.

ant.note: Life outside computers and the internet.

forms.note: There is no verb made from cyberspace.
There is no adjective made from cyberspace. Use online or cyber- words like cybersecurity.
There is no adverb made from cyberspace.

context.text: My little brother spends hours in cyberspace every evening. He chats with friends in Samarkand and plays games with people from other countries.

reviewer_note: Single-form word; cyber- words (cybercrime, cybersecurity) are compounds and left out.

corpus_definition: A violent storm with winds that turn in a circle.

forms.definition: a very strong storm with winds that turn in a circle
forms.example: The cyclone destroyed many houses in the area.

syn.note: The same kind of storm over the Atlantic Ocean.
The same kind of storm over the western Pacific Ocean.
A smaller, very fast turning wind over land.
Easy, general word for bad weather with strong wind and rain.

forms.note: There is no verb made from cyclone.

forms.definition: connected with or caused by a storm whose winds turn in a circle
forms.example: Strong cyclonic winds hit the coast last night.
forms.note: A technical word, mostly used in weather reports.

syn.note: Easy word: with strong wind and rain.

forms.note: There is no common adverb made from cyclone.

context.text: The news said a cyclone was moving towards the coast of India. Cyclonic winds and heavy rain closed the airport for two days.

reviewer_note: cyclonic is technical but real, so it is an entry, not hidden. cycle shares a Greek root but is not part of this family.

corpus_definition: Having an unusual or wrong physical shape.

forms.definition: a part of the body that has not grown in the usual shape
forms.example: The baby was born with a small deformity of the foot.

syn.note: Something not normal in the body; more medical.
A problem or fault in something, or in the body.

forms.definition: a change in the shape of something, so it is no longer right
forms.example: Heat can cause deformation of plastic pipes.

forms.definition: to change the usual shape of something so it looks wrong
forms.example: The heat from the fire deformed the metal door.

syn.note: Easy word: to turn or bend something out of shape.
Easy word: to change something straight into a curve.
To change the shape or sound of something so it is not natural.

forms.definition: having an unusual or wrong physical shape
forms.example: The metal bar was twisted and clearly deformed.
forms.note: Be careful: using it about people can sound unkind.

syn.note: Same meaning: not having the normal shape.
Changed from its natural shape.
Easy word: bent and turned out of shape.
Easy word: not straight any more.

forms.note: There is no adverb made from deformed.

context.text: The old car was in an accident and its door was badly deformed. The mechanic said the crash had deformed the metal too much to repair.

reviewer_note: Headword is a participle adjective; deform is listed as the verb it comes from. No de- affix claimed (not in the allowed table).
